lesson.title: Making DNS Answers Provably Genuine
lesson.summary: DNSSEC adds digital signatures to DNS responses so resolvers can cryptographically verify an answer really came from the legitimate zone and was not spoofed or tampered with in transit, without encrypting the query itself.
lesson.body:
Ordinary DNS was not designed with authentication in mind. When a resolver asks for the IP address behind a domain name and gets a response back, it generally has no cryptographic way to confirm that response actually originated from the domain's legitimate operator rather than from an attacker who managed to inject or spoof a convincing looking reply. A forged response that a resolver accepts as genuine can redirect a domain to an address the attacker controls, an issue often called cache poisoning. DNSSEC, DNS Security Extensions, was built to close that gap.

The mechanism is a direct application of the digital signature pattern from the previous chapter. A zone owner cryptographically signs its own DNS records using a private key it controls. For a given set of records at a given name, DNSSEC publishes an RRSIG record, which is a digital signature over that record set. The zone also publishes its public key as a DNSKEY record. A DNSSEC-validating resolver that receives a DNS answer can fetch the corresponding RRSIG and DNSKEY records and verify the signature exactly the way any digital signature is verified: recompute what the signature should cover, then check that it matches what the signer actually signed.

That still leaves a question: how does a resolver know a given zone's DNSKEY is the real one, rather than one an attacker substituted? DNSSEC answers this the same way the certificate authority chapter later in this unit answers an analogous question, by building a chain of trust up a hierarchy. Each parent zone publishes a DS, or Delegation Signer, record containing a hash of its child zone's DNSKEY, and that DS record is itself covered by the parent zone's own signature, whose validity in turn traces up to the parent's parent, and so on, all the way to the root zone. The root zone's key is the trust anchor for the entire system, distributed out of band and built into DNSSEC-validating software, and it plays a role conceptually similar to a root certificate authority that every browser is configured to trust from the start.

One distinction is important enough to state plainly, because it is easy to conflate with something DNSSEC does not do: DNSSEC authenticates that a DNS response is genuine and unmodified, it does not encrypt the query or the response. Anyone able to observe the network traffic can still see exactly which domain name is being looked up, DNSSEC does nothing to hide that. Making DNS lookups actually confidential is a separate technology entirely, encrypting the DNS transport itself, and is outside the scope of what DNSSEC was built to solve.

There is also a quiet dependency worth noting back on the very first chapter of this unit: DNSSEC signatures carry validity windows, much like the certificates covered later, so a resolver validating one needs a reasonably accurate clock to check whether a signature has expired. That is one more reason accurate time distribution through NTP matters more than it appears to on the surface.
